text: The governance model from an earlier course already decided what has to be true everywhere — no public storage, encryption at rest, every resource tagged and owned. This lesson is about something different: each environment enforces that same intent in its own native language, and maintaining one control usually means maintaining it three separate times.

Azure Policy evaluates JSON definitions with effects like deny, audit, and append, applied through management groups. AWS enforces guardrails through Service Control Policies in Organizations, backed by Config rules that continuously check resource state. On-prem has neither of those — governance there means change-control process and a CMDB, enforced by people, not an API.

Here's where that triplication actually breaks. Write the same no-public-storage rule for Azure, for AWS, and for an on-prem checklist, and six months later a new storage SKU ships on one cloud. If that cloud's independently maintained rule never gets updated to cover it, the control now exists on paper in three places but is only truly enforced in two — and nobody notices until an audit or an incident finds the gap.

This is the real case for policy-as-code. Open Policy Agent, written in Rego, or HashiCorp Sentinel, built to evaluate a Terraform plan before it applies, let you write one control once and run it against infrastructure headed for either cloud. Crucially, that doesn't retire Azure Policy or AWS Config — resources created outside Terraform still need native, continuous enforcement. Policy-as-code catches problems at provisioning time; native engines catch everything else, after the fact.

Consistency was never about identical syntax in every console — it's about the same question producing the same answer everywhere: would this violate the control we agreed on? Next lesson looks at the layer that tries to surface all of this, cost and governance both, in one dashboard — and exactly where that promise holds up and where it doesn't.
